title: About this guide
text:
This guide documents the Git and GitHub practices that the WJP team adopts as standard. Its objective is threefold:

Reduce the learning curve for new team members.
Unify criteria on how we name branches, write commits, do code review, and structure repositories.
Serve as a quick reference when someone needs to remember a command or convention.

title: About this guide
text:
Maintenance
The guide is a living document. Any team member can propose changes:

For minor corrections (errata, typos, broken links): edit directly and open a PR.
For content changes (adding a section, modifying a practice): open an issue first to discuss it, then the PR.
For policy changes (modifying a team convention): the change requires consensus, not just code review. Discuss it in the appropriate channel before opening the PR.

title: About this guide
text:
Tech stack
This site is built with Quarto, an open publishing system that supports enriched Markdown and executable code in R, Python, Julia, and JavaScript. It’s automatically published to GitHub Pages via GitHub Actions every time a merge to main happens.

title: Welcome: why this guide exists
text: This is the first blog post accompanying the WJP GitHub guide. Instead of starting with technical content, it’s worth explaining why we decided to invest time in writing this.

title: Welcome: why this guide exists
text:
The problem we’re solving
In recent months we noticed a pattern: every time someone new joined the team, we repeated the same explanations about how we work with Git. Each time slightly different, depending on who was explaining. The consequence was predictable — inconsistent conventions, recurring doubts that no one knew who to ask, and knowledge concentrated in a few people.
The solution isn’t novel: written documentation, maintained as code, accessible from anywhere.

title: Welcome: why this guide exists
section: What will live on the blog
text:
What will live on the blog
The guide is the stable reference. It covers the practices we adopt as standard.
The blog complements with:

Change announcements in policies or conventions, with their justification.
ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) — important technical decisions and why they were made.
Case studies — when something went well or badly, what we learned.
Technical notes shorter than a full section in the guide.

title: Welcome: why this guide exists
text:
How to contribute
This is an open initiative from the team. If you find errors, missing information, or want to add a post: the repository is here. The contribution rules are in About.

Welcome. Start with Basic Concepts if you’re just getting started.

title: Basic Concepts
text:
NoteBefore you start



This section is conceptual. You don’t need to install anything yet — just understand the pieces we’re going to use.

title: Basic Concepts
section: Git and GitHub are not the same thing
text:
Git and GitHub are not the same thing
Many people confuse these terms. Understanding the difference prevents conceptual errors later on.


Git
Distributed version control system

Program that runs on your computer
Records the history of changes to files
Created by Linus Torvalds in 2005
Works completely offline
Doesn’t need servers or internet



GitHub
Repository hosting platform

Web service owned by Microsoft
Visual interface for Git repositories
Pull requests, issues, permissions
Automation with GitHub Actions
Team collaboration









TipUseful analogy



Git is like Microsoft Word — it lets you write and save versions without internet.
GitHub is like Google Drive — it lets you share, comment, and collaborate with others.
You can use Word without Drive. You can use Git without GitHub.

title: Basic Concepts
text:
What problem does Git solve?
Before Git, collaborating on files looked something like this:
final_project.docx
final_project_v2.docx
final_project_v2_corrected.docx
final_project_v2_corrected_john.docx
final_project_FINAL.docx
final_project_FINAL_THIS_ONE.docx
Git solves this by recording each change as a commit — a “snapshot” of the project’s state at a given moment, with author, date, and message.

Concrete benefits


Traceability
You can see who changed what, when, and why (if the commit message is good).


Reversibility
If something broke, you can go back to any previous state without losing what came after.


Parallel collaboration
Two people can work on the same file. Git combines the changes automatically.


Safe experimentation
Create a branch to try ideas without affecting the main version.

title: Basic Concepts
text:
What does GitHub add?
Git by itself is a command-line tool. GitHub adds a complete collaboration layer:







Feature
Description




Centralized hosting
A reference place where the “official” repository lives


Web interface
Review code without cloning, browse files and histories


Pull Requests
Propose changes and discuss them before merging


Issues
Tickets for bugs, features, and tasks


Permissions
Control over who can read, write, administer


Actions
Automation for tests, deployments, and more


GitHub Pages
Free static hosting (like this site)

title: Basic Concepts
text:
Why does WJP use GitHub?


Reproducibility
Much of WJP’s work is quantitative analysis. Versioning code (R, Python) alongside documentation ensures that any result can be reproduced years later.


Collaboration
The team is distributed. Pull Requests allow reviewing colleagues’ work without needing to be in the same meeting.


Transparency
Public repositories allow third parties — academia, press, civil society — to verify methodologies.

title: Basic Concepts
text:
Alternatives to GitHub
GitHub is not the only option. Other platforms that also host Git repositories:

GitLab — popular in companies, has more integrated DevOps features
Bitbucket — by Atlassian, integrates well with Jira
Codeberg — open source and non-profit alternative

The skills you learn with Git will serve you on any platform.

title: Basic Concepts
text:
Further reading






NoteRecommended resources




Pro Git book — The official Git book, free. Chapters 1 and 2 are required reading.
GitHub Skills — Free interactive courses from GitHub.

title: Basic Concepts
text:
Next step
Now that you understand the pieces, it’s time to install the tools.
Go to Initial Setup →

title: Initial Setup
text: This section takes you from zero to having Git installed and authenticated with GitHub.

title: Initial Setup
section: Introduction to the Terminal and Bash
text:
Introduction to the Terminal and Bash
Git is a command-line tool that operates from the terminal. The commands you’ll use are written in a shell language called Bash (Bourne Again Shell).

What is Bash?
Bash is a command interpreter that allows you to interact with your computer by typing text instructions. It’s the standard shell on Unix systems (macOS, Linux) and is also available on Windows.


How to access Bash?

macOS: Open the Terminal application (found in Applications → Utilities). The default shell in modern macOS is zsh, which is compatible with Bash.
Linux: Open your distribution’s terminal. Bash is usually the default shell.
Windows: After installing Git for Windows, you’ll have access to Git Bash, an emulator that gives you a complete Bash environment.







Tip



If you ever need to explicitly switch to Bash, simply type bash in the terminal and press Enter.


All commands in this guide assume you’re in a terminal with Bash or a compatible shell (like zsh).

title: Initial Setup
text:
Installing Git

Windows
The recommended way is Git for Windows, which includes Git Bash.

Download from git-scm.com/download/win.
During installation, accept the defaults except for two points:

In “Choosing the default editor”: choose the editor you’ll use (VS Code, Notepad++, or your preference). The default (Vim) is problematic if you don’t know it.
In “Adjusting your PATH environment”: leave the middle option, “Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software”.

Verify the installation by opening Git Bash:

git --version


macOS
Three options, in order of preference:
Option A — Homebrew (recommended if you already use Homebrew):
brew install git
Option B — Xcode Command Line Tools (sufficient for most):
xcode-select --install
This installs Git along with compilers and other development utilities.
Option C — Official installer from git-scm.com/download/mac.
Verify the installation:
git --version


Linux
Use your distribution’s package manager:
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt update && sudo apt install git

# Fedora / RHEL
sudo dnf install git

# Arch
sudo pacman -S git

title: Initial Setup
text:
Authentication with GitHub CLI
The easiest way to authenticate with GitHub is using GitHub CLI (gh), GitHub’s official terminal client.

Installing GitHub CLI

macOSWindowsLinux


brew install gh
If you don’t have Homebrew installed, first install it from brew.sh:
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"


winget install GitHub.cli
Or download the installer from cli.github.com.


# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install gh

# Fedora
sudo dnf install gh

# Arch
sudo pacman -S github-cli





Authentication
Once installed, authenticate with your GitHub account:
gh auth login
The command will guide you through an interactive process:

Choose GitHub.com (not Enterprise).
Choose HTTPS as the preferred protocol.
When asked if you want to authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials, say Yes.
Choose Login with a web browser.
Copy the one-time code that appears.
Press Enter to open the browser.
Paste the code on the GitHub page and authorize.







Note



This process automatically configures Git to push and pull to GitHub repositories without asking for your password each time.




Verification
To confirm everything is working:
gh auth status
You should see something like:
github.com
  ✓ Logged in to github.com as YOUR-USERNAME
  ✓ Git operations for github.com configured to use https protocol.
  ✓ Token: gho_************************************

title: Initial Setup
text:
Auxiliary tools (optional)

Graphical client
If you prefer a graphical interface for complex tasks (reviewing large diffs, resolving conflicts):

GitHub Desktop (desktop.github.com) — simple, maintained by GitHub, sufficient for most.
GitKraken — more complete, freemium.
VS Code — has excellent built-in Git integration.







Tip



Even if you use a graphical client for day-to-day work, learn the command line. When something breaks, the GUI almost always hides what’s happening, and the solution lives in the terminal.

title: Initial Setup
text:
Next step
Now that you have Git installed and authenticated, learn to clone your first repository.

title: Cloning a Repository
text: Once you have Git installed and authenticated, the next step is to clone a repository. Cloning means creating a complete local copy of a remote repository (the one on GitHub).

title: Cloning a Repository
text:
Getting the Repository URL
Before cloning, you need the repository URL. On GitHub:

Go to the repository you want to clone.
Click the green Code button.
You’ll see two URL options: HTTPS and SSH.




Code button on GitHub

title: Cloning a Repository
text:
Method 1: Clone with HTTPS (recommended)
If you followed the setup guide and authenticated with gh auth login, this is the simplest method.

Step by step

Copy the HTTPS URL of the repository. It has this format:
https://github.com/USERNAME/REPO-NAME.git
Open the terminal and navigate to the folder where you want to save the project:
cd ~/Documents/projects
Run the git clone command followed by the URL:
git clone https://github.com/USERNAME/REPO-NAME.git
Git will create a folder with the repository name and download all the content:
Cloning into 'REPO-NAME'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 156, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (156/156), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (89/89), done.
remote: Total 156 (delta 67), reused 134 (delta 52), pack-reused 0
Receiving objects: 100% (156/156), 45.23 KiB | 1.13 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (67/67), done.
Enter the project folder:
cd REPO-NAME



Practical example
# Navigate to your projects folder
cd ~/Documents/GitHub

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/worldjusticeproject/my-project.git

# Enter the project
cd my-project

# Verify everything is okay
git status






Note



If you authenticated correctly with gh auth login, Git won’t ask for username or password. Everything should work automatically.

title: Cloning a Repository
text:
Method 2: Clone with SSH
SSH is an alternative to HTTPS that uses cryptographic keys instead of tokens. It’s useful if you prefer not to depend on GitHub CLI or if you work in an environment where SSH is the standard.

SSH Key Configuration
Before you can clone with SSH, you need to generate a key pair and add the public key to GitHub.

Step 1: Generate the key pair
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.email@worldjusticeproject.org"
When asked where to save the file, accept the default (Enter). When asked for a passphrase, you can leave it empty or set one (more secure).
This creates two files:

~/.ssh/id_ed25519 — the private key. Never share it.
~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub — the public key. This one goes to GitHub.



Step 2: Add the public key to GitHub
Copy the content of the public key:

macOSWindows (Git Bash)Linux


pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub


cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | clip


# With xclip
xclip -sel clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Or display and copy manually
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub



Then on GitHub:

Go to Settings → SSH and GPG keys.
Click New SSH key.
Give it a descriptive title (e.g., “WJP Laptop - MacBook 2025”).
Paste the public key.
Click Add SSH key.



Step 3: Verify the connection
ssh -T git@github.com
If everything is working, you’ll see:
Hi YOUR-USERNAME! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.
The message “does not provide shell access” is not an error — it’s the expected behavior.



Clone with SSH
Once the keys are configured, cloning is the same as with HTTPS but using the SSH URL:
git clone git@github.com:USERNAME/REPO-NAME.git
The SSH URL has the format git@github.com:USERNAME/REPO.git (note the colon instead of slash after github.com).


Practical example
# Clone using SSH
git clone git@github.com:worldjusticeproject/my-project.git

# Enter the project
cd my-project

# Verify
git status

title: Cloning a Repository
text:
HTTPS or SSH?








Aspect
HTTPS
SSH




Setup
Simpler with gh auth login
Requires generating and configuring keys


Security
Token stored by gh CLI
Private key on your machine


Firewalls
Works almost everywhere
Some firewalls block port 22


Recommendation
For most users
If you prefer not to use gh CLI









Tip



If you already authenticated with gh auth login, use HTTPS. It’s simpler and works just as well.

title: Cloning a Repository
text:
Clone to a specific folder
By default, git clone creates a folder with the repository name. You can specify a different name:
# Clone to a folder called "my-copy"
git clone https://github.com/USERNAME/REPO-NAME.git my-copy

title: Cloning a Repository
text:
Final verification
After cloning, verify everything is okay:
# See the repository status
git status

# See the commit history
git log --oneline -5

# See the configured remotes
git remote -v
The git remote -v command should show:
origin  https://github.com/USERNAME/REPO-NAME.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/USERNAME/REPO-NAME.git (push)
This means your local copy is connected to the repository on GitHub (called “origin”).

title: Cloning a Repository
text:
Next step
Now that you have the repository cloned, you’re ready to start working with Git.
